study.title: 2 Chronicles 3 The temple of Solomon: place, holiness, and signs of covenant
study.overview: The chapter presents the construction of the temple as the central work of Solomon's reign. The text emphasizes the place chosen by God, to the care of the measures, to the precious materials and to the symbolic elements of the sanctuary. More than describing architecture, the chapter highlights that the house of God was erected in a place of memory of divine action, with ways that communicate holiness, order, presence, and authority. The end of the chapter, with the two columns named, suggests stability and strength from the Lord Himself.

outline.title: The place chosen and the beginning of the work
outline.explanation: Solomon begins to build in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, in the place already prepared by David. The text also places the beginning of the work in the second month of the fourth year of the reign, showing that the construction takes place in a definite time and under the continuation of David's preparation.

outline.title: Measures, coatings and the most holy place
outline.explanation: The chapter describes the dimensions of the building, the portico, the internal coating in gold, the cherubim, the veil and the sanitty place. The richness of the materials and the repetition of elements of separation and glory reinforce the holiness of the house of God and the difference between the common space and the most sacred place.

outline.title: The columns before the temple
outline.explanation: The two columns placed in the entrance are given proper names, Jachin and Boaz. They function as visible signs of stability and strength, marking the entrance of the temple with the language of affirmation of God's action in favor of the house and its people.

study.context: The notes highlight that Chronicles especially values the place of the temple and its meaning. Mount Moriah is presented as the place in Jerusalem associated with the appearance of the Lord to David and the preparation made by him; some traditional Christian readings also relate it to the episode of Abraham and Isaac, but this appears as an interpretive association, not as a direct statement of this chapter. The book of Chronicles also omits the reference to the exodus present in Kings, possibly to emphasize the continuity of the bond between the people, the earth and God.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the worship of God's people is not born from isolated human initiative, but from the choice and direction of the Lord. The temple is built in a separate place, with precious materials and with a strong distinction between spaces, which communicates holiness, reverence and regulated access to the divine presence. The cherubim and the veil remember that the glory of God is real, but not banal; there is separation between the holy and the common. The columns named at the end can be read as theological signs that God establishes and sustains his home. In an evangelical reading, the text also points to the need for God to make possible the approach of his people, without diminishing the majesty of divine.

scholarViews.insight: The name Jachin can be understood as a reference to the fact that God establishes the kingdom, and Boaz as a proclamation of trust in the power of God.
The choice of Jerusalem and Mount Moriah shows that Solomon does not build anywhere; the place had already been determined by God, which gives tranquility and meaning to the project.
There is a possible textual difficulty at the time of the portico, because some old versions bring another reading; this suggests caution when treating the number as absolutely safe.

questions: What does the text teach about the importance of obeying the place and way chosen by God for worship?
How can the beauty and gold of the temple point to the holiness of God without the faith being reduced to external appearance?
How can the pillars Jachin and Boaz strengthen the trust of God's people today?
study.practice: Try to treat the worship and spiritual life with reverence, remembering that God is holy and deserves priority, order and preparation. Just as Solomon received a carefully built-in house, organize his personal devotion with constancy, zeal and submission to the Word. It is also worth cultivating trust: the power of faith is not in material symbols, but in the God who establishes and sustains his people.
study.uncertainty: The chapter is rich in architectural details, but some measures, especially the height of the portico in verse 4, present textual difficulty according to commentators. There are also symbolic readings about Moriá, cherubim and columns that are interpretative and should not be treated as unique or indisputable explanations of the text.
